group: PSI Score: Pneumonia Severity Index for CAP
question:
Patient note:
A 57-year-old man presented to the emergency department late this morning after three days of escalating shortness of breath, high fevers, and a cough that evolved from dry to producing moderate amounts of thick, blood-streaked sputum overnight; he described drenching sweats that soaked his sheets and chills so severe that his teeth chattered despite extra blankets. He lives with his spouse in a single-family ranch home and normally manages household chores, climbs two flights of stairs without difficulty, and rides an exercise bike for cardiac conditioning prescribed by his cardiologist. Past medical history is notable for a remote left hemispheric ischemic stroke two years ago that left him with no persisting weakness but resulted in daily clopidogrel therapy, and chronic systolic ventricular dysfunction attributed to a silent anterior myocardial infarction discovered five years earlier—his most recent outpatient echocardiogram six months ago documented an ejection fraction of 35 % with mild functional mitral regurgitation. He follows with primary care every four months; serum creatinine has remained in the 0.9–1.0 mg/dL range on each recent visit, and he has never required nephrology consultation or dialysis. He denies any history of cirrhosis, hepatitis, malignancy, or peripheral vascular bypass, and he has never been prescribed home oxygen, diuretics beyond his low morning dose of furosemide, or any form of renal replacement therapy. Regular medications taken the morning of presentation include carvedilol 12.5 mg twice daily, lisinopril 10 mg, furosemide 20 mg, clopidogrel 75 mg, and atorvastatin 40 mg; he had not ingested antipyretics, antibiotics, or corticosteroids during this illness. He quit smoking a decade ago after a 15-pack-year exposure, drinks an occasional beer on weekends, and denies illicit drug use. No one in his household has been ill, and he has not traveled outside the state for more than a year. Review of systems was otherwise negative for headaches, vision changes, syncope, calf pain, abdominal discomfort, dysuria, or rash. In triage he sat upright on the stretcher, speaking in short sentences but oriented to name, location, date, and circumstances without confusion. Nursing staff recorded an oral temperature of 39.3 °C, tachycardia at 118 beats per minute, tachypnea at 34 breaths per minute with nasal flaring, and an automated blood pressure of 128/76 mm Hg; pulse oximetry on ambient air registered 88 %, prompting immediate arterial sampling while he remained on room air. The arterial blood gas drawn within ten minutes showed pH 7.39, PaCO₂ 38 mm Hg, and PaO₂ 64 mm Hg. His skin was warm and flushed, conjunctiva injected but anicteric, jugular venous pressure estimated at 8 cm H₂O, and capillary refill under two seconds. Cardiac examination revealed a rapid regular S1 and S2 accompanied by a soft S3 consistent with known ventricular dysfunction, with no new murmurs or rubs. Pulmonary auscultation disclosed coarse crackles over the right lower and middle lung zones and diminished breath sounds with dullness to percussion at the extreme right base; the left lung fields were clear. Abdomen was soft, non-tender, and without hepatosplenomegaly. Extremities displayed no edema or calf tenderness, and neurologic screen revealed intact speech, symmetric strength, and normal finger-to-nose testing. Capillary glucose at the bedside was 96 mg/dL. Laboratory studies obtained before any intravenous fluids or antimicrobials demonstrated white blood cell count 15.4 × 10⁹/L with 84 % neutrophils, hematocrit 50 %, platelets 180 000/µL, sodium 129 mEq/L, potassium 4.2 mEq/L, chloride 101 mEq/L, bicarbonate 23 mEq/L, blood urea nitrogen 33 mg/dL, creatinine 1.0 mg/dL, and venous lactate 2.0 mmol/L. Troponin I was undetectable. A portable posteroanterior and lateral chest radiograph—captured while the patient remained on room air and before any therapy—displayed a dense right lower lobe consolidation with air bronchograms and blunting of the right costophrenic angle by a small meniscus of fluid, while the cardiac silhouette matched prior imaging and pulmonary vascular markings were unchanged. Electrocardiography demonstrated sinus tachycardia at 116 beats per minute without new ischemic changes or conduction block. Two sets of blood cultures, sputum Gram stain, Legionella and pneumococcal urinary antigens, and a respiratory viral multiplex swab were collected before any antibiotics. At the conclusion of the initial evaluation he had received no antipyretics, bronchodilators, vasopressors, supplemental oxygen, or intravenous fluids other than the 5 mL heparinized flush used for the arterial puncture, thereby preserving his baseline physiologic measurements at presentation.

Question: What is the patient's Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI)? You should use the patient's medical values and health status when they were first admitted to the hospital prior to any treatment.
solution:
The Pneumonia Severity Index (PSI) uses demographics, comorbidities, examination findings, and test results at presentation.
1. Demographics: A man's baseline score equals his age, so age 57 gives 57 points. He lives at home, so nursing-home residence adds 0.
2. Comorbidities: Systolic heart failure (EF 35%) adds 10; prior ischemic stroke adds 10. No malignancy, liver disease, or chronic renal disease: 0 each.
3. Examination: Respiratory rate 34/min meets the ≥30/min threshold (+20). He is oriented (0), systolic BP is 128 mm Hg, not <90 (0), temperature is 39.3°C, neither <35 nor ≥40 (0), and pulse is 118/min, not ≥125 (0).
4. Tests: BUN 33 mg/dL is ≥30 (+20); sodium 129 mEq/L is <130 (+20); radiographic pleural effusion adds 10. Arterial pH 7.39 is not <7.35 (0), glucose 96 mg/dL is not ≥250 (0), and hematocrit 50% is not <30% (0). Using the measured room-air arterial PaO₂, 64 mm Hg is not <60 (0); pulse oximetry is not scored separately.
Total = 57 + 10 + 10 + 20 + 20 + 20 + 10 = 147.
Final answer: 147
